**The Encyclopedia of Unfinished Things**

I have always been fascinated by the space between things. Not the things themselves, but the gaps. The pause between heartbeats, the breath between sentences, the blue hour between day and night when the sky doesn't know what color it wants to be. We spend so much of our lives trying to be solid, to be certain, to be *something*, but most of life actually happens in the unfinished, in-between places.

If you were to ask me to write freely — truly freely, with no prompt, no constraints, no destination — this is where my mind goes. Not to one big idea, but to a constellation of small ones that have been collecting dust on the shelves of my attention. So let me open the doors and let them wander out. Consider this an atlas of small infinities.

### 1. On Libraries That Have Never Existed

Jorge Luis Borges imagined a Library of Babel that contained every possible book. Every combination of letters, every story ever told and every story that never will be told, all housed in endless hexagonal rooms. It's a beautiful and terrifying idea because it suggests that meaning is not scarce. In fact, meaning is drowned in noise.

But I think about a different library. A smaller, sadder, more human library.

The Library of Unwritten Books. The books that lived entirely inside someone's head for decades and never made it to paper. The novel a woman plotted while washing dishes for thirty years, perfect in her mind, with characters more real than her neighbors, who died without writing a single chapter. The memoir a man rehearsed on his commute every morning, editing the story of his childhood until it shone, but never trusting anyone enough to hear it. The poetry collection that existed as a feeling in a teenager's chest that he didn't have the words for yet, and by the time he did, the feeling had changed shape.

That library is larger than the Library of Congress. It contains more masterpieces than we will ever read. And unlike Borges' library, which is infinite and therefore indifferent, this library is finite and heartbreaking because each book disappears forever when its author does.

We think of writing as creating something from nothing. But maybe it's more like rescue work. You are pulling a fragile, half-formed world out of the dark water of yourself before it drowns. Most worlds drown.

I sometimes wonder what civilization would look like if we had access to that library. If we could briefly wander its aisles. How many of our problems were already solved in a book that was never written? How many lonely people would have discovered that someone else felt exactly the same way they did, in a book that was never published?

This is why I think anyone who finishes anything — a bad novel, a clumsy painting, a wobbly table — has performed a small miracle. They have moved something from the infinite invisible library into the visible one. The quality almost doesn't matter. The translation itself is the triumph.

### 2. The Problem With Maps

When I was nine, I had a large, laminated world map on my bedroom wall. I loved it with an intensity that now seems religious. I would trace the shipping routes with my finger, memorize capitals, invent stories for the tiny specks of islands in the Pacific I was sure no one ever visited. The map made the world feel knowable. Containable. Neat.

Then one day my teacher showed us a globe, and then, more devastatingly, different projections of the same globe. Mercator versus Peters versus Robinson. Suddenly Greenland was not the size of Africa. Suddenly the map on my wall was not the world, but an opinion about the world. A useful lie.

We live by maps like that. Mental maps.

We have a map for success: go to school, get good grades, get a good job, get promoted, buy a house, retire. We have a map for relationships: meet, date, marry, children. We have a map for a day: morning routine, productivity, evening wind-down. These maps are not the territory of a human life. They are projections. They distort something to make something else legible. The Mercator map makes navigation easier but makes Greenland monstrous. The "success" map makes ambition legible but makes rest look like failure.

Most of our anxiety, I think, comes from confusing the map for the territory. We feel guilty when our actual, messy, globe-shaped life doesn't match the flat, clean map we were given. We think we are lost. We aren't lost. We are just off-map. And off-map is where all the actual life is — the forests, the deserts, the people who never agreed to be a symbol.

Lately I've been trying to draw my own maps, loosely, in pencil. A map where north is not "more achievement" but "more aliveness." Where distance is not measured in money or milestones but in how often I am surprised. It is a terrible map for navigation. You can't use it to explain yourself at reunions. But it gets me to more interesting places.

There is an old cartographer's trick: they used to draw sea monsters in the unexplored parts of the ocean. *Here be dragons.* We treat the unknown parts of our lives like that — with fear. But what if the dragons are just undiscovered coastlines? What if the most accurate map you could ever make of your life would be mostly blank space with the words *Here be wonder* written lightly in the margins?

### 3. A Brief Natural History of Attention

Attention is the only true currency we have. You can have all the money and time in the world, but if your attention is shattered, you are poor.

A hundred years ago, attention was a river. It moved relatively slowly, in one direction. You could put your boat in and float for a while. A book for an afternoon. A conversation for an evening.

Fifty years ago, it became a busy street. Lots of cars, stoplights, people shouting from storefronts. You had to look both ways constantly. Television, radio, magazines.

Now it is a swarm of bees. Or maybe a broken mirror with a thousand reflections, each one shouting *Look at me!* It does not move in one direction anymore. It vibrates. It darts. It never lands long enough to pollinate anything.

We talk about the "attention economy" as if it is an economy that trades in attention. But it is more accurate to say it is an economy that *mines* attention the way an earlier economy mined coal. It extracts it, refines it, burns it for energy elsewhere, and leaves the source hollowed out and polluted. Your ability to notice a single leaf for ten seconds without needing to photograph it or share it is not a trivial skill. It is an endangered ecosystem.

I have been practicing a small rebellion. Every day, I try to give my uninterrupted attention to one useless, beautiful thing for five minutes. Not meditating on it to become more productive. Not observing it to post about mindfulness. Just looking. The way the steam from my tea catches the morning light and becomes briefly visible, then invisible. The way my dog's ears twitch in his sleep as he chases dream-squirrels. The sound of rain hitting different surfaces — the metal railing *tink*, the leaves *shush*, the pavement *hiss*.

It is shockingly difficult at first. Your brain, trained by the swarm, will try to pull you away. *We should be doing something. We should be optimizing.* But if you stay, something softens. Time, which had been chopped into frantic TikTok-sized fragments, begins to stretch and pool again, like water after a dam breaks.

Attention is not just about focus. It is about love. As the poet Mary Oliver wrote, "Attention is the beginning of devotion." You cannot love anything you do not truly notice. And you cannot notice anything if you are constantly being pulled to notice everything.

### 4. The Museum of Lost Socks and Other Mysteries

There is a place in my house that functions as a museum of small disappearances. The junk drawer. Every house has one. Inside it: three different kinds of batteries that may or may not be dead, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed in 2019, a single earring, a key that opens nothing we can remember, a tangle of cables for devices we no longer own, and of course, the lone sock whose partner vanished in the dryer dimension.

We laugh about these things, but they point to a quiet, ongoing entropy that defines domestic life. Things want to fall apart. Order wants to dissolve into chaos. Not dramatically, but sock by sock.

The second law of thermodynamics is the most poetic law in physics. It says that in any closed system, disorder tends to increase. The universe is slowly moving from order to disorder, from low entropy to high entropy. Your bedroom becoming messy is not a moral failure. It is the universe doing what the universe does.

And yet, against this cosmic tide, we make beds. We fold laundry. We wash dishes knowing they will be dirty again in twelve hours. We sweep floors that will gather dust again by tomorrow. Why?

Albert Camus said we must imagine Sisyphus happy — the man condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only to watch it roll back down. I think the person who does the dishes every night understands Sisyphus better than any philosopher. It is absurd. It will never stay done. And we do it anyway. And sometimes, while the warm water runs over our hands and the window is dark outside, we feel a strange, quiet peace in the repetition.

Caring for things that will fall apart anyway is not futile. It is the entire point. It is how we say: *I was here. I loved this small corner of chaos enough to try to make it orderly for a little while, even though I knew I would fail.*

My grandmother used to darn socks. She would sit in her chair with a wooden egg inside the sock and weave thread over the hole until it disappeared. It would have been cheaper and faster to buy new socks. But she wasn't just fixing a sock. She was practicing a philosophy: that what is worn thin can be made whole again, that what is broken is not necessarily to be discarded.

We don't darn socks much anymore. We throw them away. We are richer in socks and poorer in that kind of patience. I wonder what else we throw away that could have been mended.

### 5. How to Time Travel Without a Machine

You don't need a machine. You have always been a time traveler.

Memory is time travel to the past, but not like watching a film. It is more like archaeology. You don't retrieve a perfect copy; you reconstruct ruins. Every time you remember your childhood kitchen, you are rebuilding it from fragments — the smell of coffee, the linoleum pattern, the sound of a chair scraping. The kitchen you remember today is slightly different from the kitchen you remembered ten years ago, because *you* are different. The past is not a fixed place we visit. It is a story we retell ourselves, and the story changes as the storyteller changes.

Anticipation is time travel to the future. Worry is particularly vivid time travel — we create a future in such high resolution that our body reacts as if it is already happening. The heart races for a presentation that is still three days away. We suffer a hundred imagined failures that never arrive.

And nostalgia — nostalgia is time travel for a place that never existed. It is a past bathed in golden light, edited to remove the boredom, the anxiety, the mosquito bites that were actually there. We don't miss the past. We miss the way we were able to feel in the past, before we knew how hard everything was.

The only time we are not time traveling is right now. And right now is the only place where life is actually happening. That's the great cosmic joke. Our most sophisticated mental abilities — memory and imagination — are also what constantly pull us out of the only moment that is real.

I am not saying we should live only in the present like some blissed-out guru. The past has lessons and the future needs plans. But I am saying it is worth noticing how often you are away. If you added up all the hours you have spent in 2018 or 2027 while your body was sitting in 2026, you would be amazed at how little time you've spent *here*.

One small practice: several times a day, ask yourself gently, *Where am I?* Not geographically, but temporally. Am I here, feeling the chair under me, hearing the air conditioner hum? Or am I in a future argument, a past regret? Just asking the question tends to quietly bring you back, like calling a dog's name. You don't need to scold the dog for wandering. Just call it home.

We are all time travelers. The trick is learning to come home more often.

### 6. An Incomplete List of Things That Are Worth Doing Badly

We have become obsessed with doing things well. Optimally. With mastery. If you can't be good at it, why do it? This is a catastrophic idea.

Here is a list of things that are worth doing badly, especially badly at first, and perhaps forever:

Singing, even if you are out of tune. Dancing, even if you have no rhythm. Drawing, even if your people look like potatoes. Writing poetry, even if it is cliché. Playing a musical instrument, even if you only know three chords. Speaking a new language, even if you sound like a child. Cooking, even if you burn the garlic. Gardening, even if you kill half the plants. Meditating, even if you can't stop thinking. Loving people, even if you are awkward at it.

Most of the things that make life joyful are not worth doing because you are good at them. They are worth doing because they make you feel more alive. A child does not dance to be excellent. A child dances because the music makes her body want to move. We train that out of ourselves when we start to believe that every activity must be judged, ranked, and potentially monetized.

Perfectionism is a thief. It tells you that you cannot share your song until it is flawless, which means you never share it at all. It tells you that the amateur — literally, from the Latin *amare*, to love — is inferior to the expert. But the lover may understand the thing more deeply than the expert who has turned love into labor.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that finds beauty in imperfection and impermanence. A cracked bowl mended with gold. An uneven glaze on a tea cup. The beauty is not despite the flaw, but because of it. The flaw is proof that a human hand made it, that it has lived a life.

Give yourself permission to be a glorious amateur. Your badly sung song, your lopsided loaf of bread, your wobbly yoga pose — these are not failures. They are evidence that you are participating instead of just spectating. And the world needs fewer perfect spectators and more enthusiastic, imperfect participants.

So tonight, do something you are bad at, for no other reason than that you like doing it. Notice how freedom feels. Notice how it doesn't matter.

---

If you've read this far, thank you for lending me your attention for a little while. In the swarm, that is a gift.

I don't have a neat conclusion. I told you — I'm interested in the unfinished. If I were to tie this all up with a moral, it would betray the point. Life doesn't conclude. It just continues, messy and entropic and beautiful, until it doesn't.

Instead, I will leave you where I started: in the in-between. Between what you expected this to be and what it actually was. Between the person you were when you started reading and the person you are now, a few thousand words later, slightly different in some tiny, unmeasurable way.

May your library of unwritten books get a little smaller this year. May your maps be drawn in pencil. May you notice one useless, beautiful thing today for five whole minutes. May you mend something instead of throwing it away. May you come home to the present moment more often. And may you do at least one thing badly and joyfully before the day is over.

The rest is blank space. Here be wonder.
